analysis.one_liner: Restricts fees, prepayment penalties, balloon payments, single-premium insurance, and forced arbitration in high-cost home mortgages.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in committee for two years with no markup and no vote, despite 35 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have tightened federal rules on high-cost home mortgages: lenders would have to verify that a borrower can actually afford the loan, disclose in plain language that the rate is unusually high and that the home is at risk, and drop practices like balloon payments, financed single-premium credit insurance, and clauses forcing disputes into private arbitration. It would also have capped the fees a lender can finance into the loan, limited prepayment penalties, raised penalties for violations, and given borrowers more time to sue. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners taking or refinancing high-cost mortgages — typically people with weak credit who borrow against their homes — would gain clearer warnings, cheaper loans without padded fees and insurance, loans they are actually able to repay, and stronger tools to fight back in court or stop a foreclosure. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Requires lenders to verify each borrower's income, obligations, and employment and confirm they can make the scheduled payments before making a high-cost mortgage, verified independently rather than on the borrower's say-so.

Requires plain-language disclosures telling the borrower the rate is much higher than most people pay, that the chance of losing the home is much higher, and that a cheaper loan may be available, plus referrals to approved credit counseling.
Bans all balloon payments in these loans and limits prepayment penalties to the first 24 months and to no more than 3% of the loan.
Caps the points and fees a lender can finance into the loan at the greater of 3% of the loan or $600, and bars financing prepayment penalties owed on the old loan being refinanced.

Prohibits lenders from financing single-premium credit life, disability, unemployment, or property insurance in the loan — products added to the balance that earn the borrower little and drain home equity.
Bars contract terms that force disputes into arbitration or other nonjudicial procedures, preserving the borrower's right to sue.

Raises civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation plus class-action amounts, extends the deadline to sue over violations to three years, and lets a borrower raise rescission as a defense in a foreclosure.
Requires lenders and their successors to report the borrower's complete payment history to credit bureaus, so paying the loan builds credit rather than vanishing from the record.

analysis.who_pays: Subprime mortgage lenders and mortgage brokers, who would lose the ability to load loans with financed fees, prepayment penalties, single-premium insurance premiums, and no-sue arbitration clauses; credit insurance sellers would lose a captive sales channel, and some borrowers would find fewer lenders willing to make high-cost loans at all.

drawbacks.text: The counseling and verification requirements would add cost and delay to every high-cost loan, and some lenders would simply stop serving that market, leaving some subprime borrowers with fewer options or no loan at all.

The high-cost definition is broad — any first mortgage more than 6 points over the Treasury rate, and any loan with points and fees over 5% — so higher compliance costs would fall on some loans that are not abusive, not just on predatory ones.

Making loan purchasers liable for claims against the original lender (for home-improvement financing) could reduce the amount of money investors are willing to buy these loans for, tightening credit further.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections aim squarely at practices that strip home equity — financed fees and insurance, balloon payments, serial refinancing, and arbitration clauses — and the bill's own text shows it anticipated the industry's standard evasion moves, including bans on restructuring loans to dodge the rules. The real cost is access: some marginal borrowers would pay less but also get approved less often, and tighter assignee liability could shrink the market for these loans. On balance the trade favors borrowers, because the practices restricted are precisely the ones that end in losing the home.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, then to its financial institutions subcommittee, and nothing further happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John LaFalce introduced the bill on March 15, 2001 with 10 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, and on April 2, 2001 to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit.
The bill received no further committee action, no markup, and no floor vote during the rest of the Congress.
By the end of the Congress the bill had 35 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats; none from the Republican majority that chaired the committee it sat in.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subprime lenders, mortgage brokers, and credit insurance sellers kept every practice the bill would have banned — financed fees, prepayment penalties, single-premium insurance, forced arbitration — and high-cost lending continued unchecked into the housing boom that followed.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run Financial Services Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill attacks the core revenue devices of high-cost lending: financed points and fees, prepayment penalties, balloon payments, and serial refinancing with new penalties. Lenders profit from these at the direct expense of borrowers' home equity, which is why their interest ran against the bill's protections.

Broker compensation of any kind would count toward the points-and-fees cap, and brokers originating high-cost loans would be regulated as creditors. Brokers' earnings in this market came from fees stacked on the borrower's loan.

The bill bans financing single-premium credit life, disability, unemployment, and property insurance in the mortgage — a captive market in which expensive policies were added to the loan balance and drained home equity while providing little real benefit.

industries.industry: Investors and securitizers buying high-cost loans
industries.note: Assignees would inherit the borrower's claims and defenses against the original lender, lowering what the loans could be sold for, but the mandatory payment-history reporting would make the loans easier to evaluate and service.
Lenders would have to give borrowers referrals to HUD-approved counseling before closing, creating a mandated touchpoint for counseling services that serve borrowers.
